extracted.intended_audience: educators, university policymakers, and the educated public interested in higher-education reform
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and practical criteria for what counts as genuine education and how universities should educate (balance of humanities and sciences, methods of instruction, depth vs breadth, role of community and self-education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of education
rubrics_metrics.description: "Education is a high word; it is the preparation for knowledge, and it is the imparting of knowledge in proportion to that preparation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education requires both 'intellectual eyes' (capacities) and objects (knowledge) and cannot be achieved passively or haphazardly; it is the preparation for knowing, not mere amusement or pastime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recreations and accomplishments are not education
rubrics_metrics.description: "Recreations are not education; accomplishments are not education."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: drawing, fencing, stuffing birds, playing stringed instruments, or a superficial acquaintance with botany or conchology—these are elegant pastimes or accomplishments useful as resources or amusements but do not form or cultivate the intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth over superficial breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: "A thorough knowledge of one science and a superficial acquaintance with many, are not the same thing; a smattering of a hundred things or a memory for detail, is not a philosophical or comprehensive view."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The modern error is forcing so much undigested knowledge that students retain nothing; smattering in many branches is shallowness, not enlargement. Prefer grounded, finished study in subjects rather than many badly learned ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against passive/mechanical learning (printing-press fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: "What the steam engine does with matter, the printing press is to do with the mind...the population is to be passively, almost unconsciously enlightened, by the mere multiplication and dissemination of volumes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disputes the notion that mere availability and multiplication of books or lectures produces education; active, conscious effort and preparation by the learner are required—education cannot be received in sleep or by haphazard means.

rubrics_metrics.name: University as alma mater with residence and tutorial supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: "A university is, according to the usual designation, an alma mater, knowing her children one by one, not a foundry, or a mint, or a treadmill."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favours universities that provide residence and tutorial superintendence over systems that dispense degrees by wide-range examinations without residence or personal instruction; personal tutelage and community supervision are central to intellectual discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of social/peer learning and 'genius loci'
rubrics_metrics.description: When a multitude of young men...come together and freely mix with each other, they are sure to learn one from another...the conversation of all is a series of lectures to each...it will embody a specific idea...a self-perpetuating tradition, or a genius loci.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The college community itself is an educational agent: diverse peers interacting produce continual informal instruction, shared standards of judgment, and a unifying intellectual atmosphere that complements formal teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-education preferable to poor formal teaching but has limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Shut your college gates against the votary of knowledge, throw him back upon the searchings and the efforts of his own mind; he will gain by being spared an entrance into your babel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-education can yield more thought and true enlargement than an ill-conceived institutional system, but unassisted learners risk eccentricity, gaps in foundational knowledge, inability to converse, and overconfidence; balance is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture requires knowing the best thought and said—includes sciences and humanities
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the best which has been thought and said in the world...this includes Greek, Roman, and Eastern antiquity and also what modern nations have done (e.g., Copernicus, Galileo, Newton, Darwin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that 'literature' in the broad sense includes scientific works (Euclid, Newton). A genuine culture combines knowledge of belles lettres with knowledge of major scientific achievements; both are part of the intellectual outfit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of natural science for the habit of dealing with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "The habit of dealing with facts, which is given by the study of nature, is...an excellent discipline."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural science trains observation and experiment—making knowledge demonstrable and 'real' (e.g., seeing that wax converts to carbonic acid and water). This empirical habit is a valuable component of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must address multiple human powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Human nature is built up by powers: the power of conduct, the power of intellect and knowledge, the power of beauty, and the power of social life and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should balance and relate these powers; reformers who make natural science the chief part of education may neglect other necessary faculties (moral, aesthetic, social).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning should be systematic and go to original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: "I call all teaching 'scientific' which is systematically laid out and followed up to its original sources...a knowledge of classical antiquity is scientific when the remains of classical antiquity are correctly studied in the original languages."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endorses rigorous, source-based study (e.g., classical studies in original languages) rather than superficial or decorative familiarity; 'scientific' teaching equals systematic, source-grounded instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise higher faculties over mere memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not extol the cultivation of that intellect which is the prey...of barren facts...I am not denying that a strong and ready memory is in itself a real treasure...they constitute no type of the results at which it aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memory and detailed factual knowledge have value, but education's aim is to cultivate higher intellectual faculties (judgment, philosophy, synthesis). Enlarging memory at the expense of these faculties is no gain.
